review_design_self_description: systematic review (PRISMA 2020 guidelines with narrative thematic synthesis)
methodological_notes: 1. Design vs. execution: Although self-described as a PRISMA 2020 systematic review with OSF registration, registration was performed retrospectively during peer-review revision (June 2026), no risk-of-bias/quality tool was applied, only 70 total records were retrieved across 5 databases (including Google Scholar) spanning 2000-2025, and findings are presented as an exploratory scoping/narrative thematic synthesis across environmental contamination (28 studies), public health/AMR (10), household coping (5), seasonal surface water (7), and governance (8). 2. Narrow Criterion 2 audit: Governance and regulatory gaps form one of the review's three explicit research questions (RQ3; Section 3.5; Section 4.3), covering overlapping agency mandates, weak regulatory oversight of informal tanker markets/private water vendors (Sapkota 2014 [28]), and groundwater transition from open-access to state-regulated resource (Pandey & Kazama 2023 [33]). However, legal/tenure/tariff/regulatory mechanisms are treated only as high-level descriptive themes secondary to biophysical water contamination monitoring, justifying 'borderline_narrow_c2'. 3. Included-studies accounting anomaly: The paper reports 45 included studies, provides no study-by-study table or supplement (Table 1 explicitly gives only 'Representative Studies' by domain), and lists only 49 total references in the entire bibliography. Subtracting 5 non-Nepal conceptual/guideline references ([34] Jepson 2017, [35] Wutich 2017, [36] Balazs & Ray 2014, [37] Page 2021 PRISMA, [45] Suraifi 2023) leaves 44 Nepal/Kathmandu references in total: 38 cited in Table 1/Results (extracted above; note [29] is itself a review and [5, 21, 30, 32] are online media/NGO pages) plus 6 cited only in Introduction or Discussion ([11] Khatiwada 2002, [44] Khare 2025, [46] Katuwal 2012 PhD thesis, [47] Shrestha 2023 review, [48] Chattopadhyay 2025 scoping review, and [49] Shrestha et al. 2024 IWMI blog—notably the only IWMI source matching Section 2.2's search description), while conceptual paper [36] (Balazs & Ray 2014) is erroneously cited in Table 1 under 'Representative Studies' (38 + 6 + [36] = 45). No literal DOI strings are printed in the Reference list (only '[CrossRef]' links).

review_design_self_description: systematic review (PRISMA 2020 qualitative thematic synthesis / SLR)
methodological_notes: Although titled a PRISMA 2020 'Systematic review' (SLR), this paper is methodologically a low-rigour qualitative thematic/scoping synthesis (NVivo 12) of 20 heterogeneous sources including empirical surveys/case studies, secondary policy commentaries, and a book chapter, making AMSTAR 2 only borderline-applicable and yielding Critically Low confidence (5 critical flaws: Q2, Q4, Q7, Q9, Q13). Multiple internal reporting anomalies exist: (1) Section 2 lists 5 databases/platforms whereas Section 3.1 lists 8 (including publisher platforms Elsevier/ScienceDirect counted separately and ResearchGate); (2) Section 3.5 states 62 database records yielded 24 unique records after deduplication, whereas Section 4 states 62 database records plus 8 citation-chasing records (70 total) yielded the same 24 records; (3) Google Scholar was truncated at 20 hits; (4) the search window began in January 2002 even though Jal Jeevan Mission launched in 2019, resulting in pre-JJM or non-JJM inclusions such as a 2019 study of women fetching water in Kenya (Agesa & Agesa [13], never cited in the Results); (5) Table 1 S. No. 10 ('Kumar & Goyal [9]') erroneously duplicates reference number [9] (Ranjeet Kumar 2024) and lacks a reference list entry; (6) Table 3 research method counts sum to 23 across 20 included studies; and (7) PRISMA 2020 (Page et al. 2021) is cited twice as Ref [1] and Ref [4]. On scope (Criterion 2), the review is primarily a broad programme evaluation of JJM (socio-economic/gender, health, infrastructure), touching only secondarily on local administrative governance (Gram Panchayat roles, contractor/local-government responsibility ambiguity, and missing grievance redressal mechanisms), so it is rated borderline_narrow_c2. References [25]-[32] appear only as external comparative/discussion citations in Sections 6.2, 6.4, 6.6, and 7 and are excluded from the 20 synthesized studies in Table 1.

review_design_self_description: systematic review (PRISMA 2020 deductive qualitative and bibliometric thematic review of 470 journal articles, book chapters, and reviews)
methodological_notes: Fanaian et al. (2025) is classified under WIREs Water's "SYSTEMATIC REVIEW" rubric and follows PRISMA 2020 screening mechanics across six databases (2299 records -> 1935 deduplicated abstracts -> 542 full texts -> 470 included publications; protocol published in ANU Open Repository as Fanaian 2024). Methodologically, however, it functions as a broad systematic scoping/thematic mapping review rather than an empirical effectiveness review: (1) its search string was strictly limited to "water justice" OR "water equity" and explicitly excluded studies framed solely around "human right to water" or "water access"; (2) its 470-item corpus pools primary empirical studies alongside theoretical essays, edited-volume chapters, and other secondary reviews (e.g., De Guzman et al. 2023; Leonard et al. 2023; Schmidt 2023; Zuniga-Teran et al. 2021; Rusca and Cleaver 2022; Gupta et al. 2022a/b — omitted from included_primary_studies above to avoid review-on-review conflation); (3) no individual study table or bibliography of the 470 included records is printed in the PDF or shared as open data ("Data sharing is not applicable"), and Annex Tables 1–5 in Supporting Information contain only thematic/country aggregations; and (4) no risk-of-bias appraisal was conducted, yielding Critically Low confidence under AMSTAR 2 (critical flaws on Q7, Q9, and Q13). Narrow Criterion 2 is borderline because a substantive subset of synthesized primary studies examines legal, regulatory, tariff, shutoff, ownership, and slum-tenure WASH rules (e.g., Bae et al. 2023 on SDWA enforcement; Stewart 2022 on mandatory consolidation; Lubeck-Schricker et al. 2023 on legal exclusion in Mumbai slums; Zhang et al. 2022a/b on public vs. private water pricing and shutoff moratoria), whereas the overall corpus spans river basins, irrigation, hydropower, lithium mining, tourism, and non-empirical theory.

review_design_self_description: systematic review (descriptive thematic/scoping-style synthesis of observational, practitioner, and case-study literature)
methodological_notes: Although self-described as a PRISMA systematic review of peer-reviewed journals (Jan 2002-Dec 2021) with 37 included articles, the review functions methodologically as a descriptive scoping/thematic mapping synthesis (counting frequency of themes across 17 observational studies, 10 practitioner papers, and 10 case studies, with zero risk-of-bias appraisal). Three major internal reporting anomalies affect primary-study tracking: (1) No Characteristics of Included Studies table or list of the 37 included studies is printed in the PDF (nor is one cited in the Supplementary Material, which only references Tables S1 and S2 for eligibility criteria and search terms), and Results Section 3 cites ~48 primary/case/practitioner FS-emptying studies in SSA, South and Southeast Asia without distinguishing the formal 37-study sample from supplemental discussion citations (including 2022 papers outside the 2002-2021 search window); (2) despite claiming to restrict to peer-reviewed journals, Section 3.2 explicitly counts grey/practitioner reports and conference papers (e.g., Eawag and Sandec 2006; Thye et al. 2009; Chowdry and Kone 2012; Hawkins et al. 2014) among the included studies; and (3) Section 3.2 states there were no experimental studies, yet Section 3.3.2 cites Peletz et al. (2020), an experimental comparison of pit-emptying services in Kisumu, Kenya. Regarding Narrow Criterion 2, the review is borderline: its primary scope is broad technological and operational challenges of FS emptying, though institutional/regulatory rules (criminalization of manual emptying, licensing/permits, unequal taxation, municipal regulation, PPP lease contracts, and tariff subsidies) constitute a substantial sub-theme (Section 3.4.5, 14/37 studies; Section 3.5.1, PPPs).

review_design_self_description: systematic realist review (combined systematic and realist review of peer-reviewed and grey literature)
methodological_notes: 1. Hybrid Design & AMSTAR 2 Fit: Castleden et al. (2017) describe their study as a combined 'systematic and realist review (SRR)' examining the 'extent, range, and nature' of academic and grey literature on integrative Indigenous and Western knowledge approaches to water research and management in Canada (1979–Aug 2015), using a 33-item Context-Mechanism-Outcome reporting tool co-created with a National Advisory Committee and Water Gathering participants. AMSTAR 2 is borderline for this scoping/realist hybrid, and the review scores Critically Low due to lack of a registered protocol, exclusion of French-language Canadian literature without methodological justification, non-duplicate partitioned extraction, no list of excluded studies, no table of included studies, no risk-of-bias/quality assessment, and no conflict-of-interest statement (despite co-authors' own primary studies—Daley 2014, Harper 2011, Martin 2007—being included). 2. Screening Flow Discrepancies: Figure 1 is blank in the published PDF, and the narrative screening numbers on p. 13 do not reconcile cleanly (226 academic records retrieved -> 29 included + 37 excluded + 36 full-text reviewed = 102 accounted for, followed by 'a total of 40 included; 64 excluded' = 104; plus 53 grey-literature documents yielding 12 reports and 11 theses/dissertations, for a reported total of 279 reviewed and 63 included). 3. Incomplete Identification of Included Studies: No included-studies table, appendix, or bibliography marker is printed; 57 of the 63 included records are identifiable via inline citations in Findings (pp. 16–21), whereas several Canadian water papers in the Reference list (e.g., Basdeo & Bharadwaj 2013, Mascarenhas 2007, Phare 2011, Sanderson et al. 2015, Walkem 2007) appear only in the Introduction or Discussion and cannot be verified as formally included. Note also that the printed DOI for Gearheard et al. (2006) on p. 29 ('10.3390/ijerph13050505') is a copy-paste error duplicating Galway (2016). 4. Narrow Criterion 2 Fit: Borderline—only 26% of included studies focused on drinking water and ~14 examined water governance, treaty/Aboriginal water rights, operator certification, or First Nations drinking-water legislative frameworks, while the main review object is methodological/epistemological knowledge co-production across all water environments (including Arctic sea ice, marine planning, fish/forests, and watersheds).

review_design_self_description: targeted systematic review following PRISMA 2020 guidelines (with self-noted scoping nature and narrative PICO synthesis)
methodological_notes: Substantive scope passes narrow Criterion 2 (examines tariff-setting regulations, prepaid vs. postpaid tariff rules, cross-subsidization, private/cooperative/community utility ownership and governance models in rural piped water supply). However, methodological quality under AMSTAR 2 is Critically Low due to multiple critical flaws (no registered protocol, single-database Scopus-only search yielding 49 hits and 8 included studies, no excluded-studies list, inadequate adapted-CASP RoB tool, and contradictory RoB integration). Forensic audit also reveals severe editorial/reporting defects: (1) p. 6 erroneously refers to 'the fifteen articles... presented in Table 2' whereas Table 2 and the entire review include 8 studies; (2) Abstract and p. 11 report 5 Moderate RoB and 3 Low RoB studies, contradicting Table 5 (p. 12), which rates 7 studies Moderate and only 1 (Grant et al., 2020) Low; (3) Table 5 contains unedited second-person LLM/reviewer prompt text ('in your summary is limited', 'acceptable in your description'); (4) the opening paragraph of the Discussion (p. 12) prints raw manuscript-template instructions verbatim; (5) Table 3 (p. 9) attributes ~15% coverage increase and >90% cost coverage from bank loans/cross-subsidy to Kumasi (2018) (duplicating Meleg 2012's outcomes), contradicting Table 4 (p. 10) which notes banks in Ghana granted zero loans to WSMTs; and (6) one of the 8 included studies (Walters & Javernick-Will, 2015) is itself a systematic literature review of 97 articles rather than a primary empirical study. Note that journal header prints Journal of People, Plants, and Environment (JPPE) rather than J Korean Soc Environ Eng.

review_design_self_description: Self-described PRISMA systematic review (in practice a hybrid/pseudo-systematic qualitative narrative policy review including both empirical and non-empirical sources)
methodological_notes: Although the author self-describes the paper as a PRISMA 'systematic review' (pp. 1, 3) reporting 65 identified records, 10 duplicates removed, 19 excluded at screening, and 36 included documents (p. 8), the study is methodologically a single-author pseudo-systematic narrative essay of Critically Low quality under AMSTAR 2. First, no protocol, PICO framework, duplicate screening/extraction, excluded-study list, risk-of-bias appraisal, or conflict-of-interest disclosure is provided, and candidate journals were arbitrarily filtered by Web of Science impact factor (p. 4). Second, eligibility criteria are internally contradictory—claiming 'Both empirical and non-empirical sources were chosen' while immediately requiring 'quantitative approaches on the issue at hand with an analytical rather than descriptive methodology' and data 'taken from the US government' (p. 4)—yet the synthesis relies heavily on Gizmodo/ScienceDaily news posts, books, UN/WHO reports, conceptual essays, and secondary reviews (e.g., Llausàs & Saurí 2017; March et al. 2012; Rozema et al. 2016; Saurí 2013). Third, Table 1 ('Literature analyzed', pp. 5-7) was embedded as a non-OCR raster image in the source PDF so its 36 rows are blank in extracted text; meanwhile, 52 distinct works are cited across the thematic synthesis sections (pp. 8-13, extracted above separately from Introduction-only citations), with pervasive citation misattribution (e.g., citing Spanish conservation-theatre, EU 30% climate-target, and Australian suburban-garden studies for US rural aquifer, Florida wastewater, and California desalination claims). Substantively, it is borderline on narrow Criterion 2 because it discusses public vs. investor-owned/cooperative/self-supply ownership, reserved water rights, regulatory oversight, tariffs/cost recovery, and federal farm-bill conservation subsidies, but conflates agricultural land-stewardship programs (CSP, EQIP) with household rural drinking-water governance without rigorous empirical synthesis.

review_design_self_description: systematic review / systematic literature review (self-described as a hybrid systematic and backward-searching review using thematic analysis)
methodological_notes: 1. Scope & Criterion 2/3 Assessment: Substantively, S344 squarely addresses narrow Criterion 2 by examining legal, contractual, and regulatory rules governing urban water access in Jakarta—specifically the 1998–2023 Public-Private Partnership (PPP) concession contracts, the 2023 remunicipalization handover to public utility PAM JAYA, regulatory failure to enforce groundwater extraction bans, tariff governance, and informal settlement exclusion. Methodologically (Criterion 3), although self-described as a 'systematic literature review' (and 'hybrid systematic and backward-searching review') with search terms, Table 2 eligibility criteria, and a PRISMA diagram, it functions as a critically flawed qualitative/scoping-style thematic narrative rather than a rigorous systematic synthesis. 2. Severe Reporting Discrepancy on Included Studies: The paper claims n=31 included studies (27 contemporary 2010–2024 studies from Google Scholar plus 4 pre-2010 foundational studies from backward snowballing; p. 5 & Table 3), yet provides no study-by-study characteristics table or appendix, and the entire References list (p. 13) contains only 14 entries total. Of those 14 references, only 8 ([4], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [13], [14]) are cited in Section 3 Results/Discussion as synthesized studies; 3 others ([3] Fulazzaky 2014, [5] World Bank 2006, [11] Takagi et al. 2016) appear only in Section 1 Introduction or Table 1 illustrative indicators, and 3 ([1], [2], [12]) are general urban or methodological citations. Consequently, at least 20–23 of the claimed 31 included studies are completely unidentifiable and uncited. 3. Additional Editorial/Methodological Red Flags: Single-author screening and coding without protocol registration or risk-of-bias assessment; reliance solely on Google Scholar; duplicate section headings in Section 1.1/1.3, 4.1/4.2, and 4.2.1/4.2.2; and unedited prompt/placeholder prose printed beneath Figure 1 ('The diagram would show...').

1. Review Design & Scope: Self-described JBI scoping review (Peters et al., 2020) synthesizing qualitative and mixed-methods peer-reviewed journal articles (2000-2022, English) on access inequalities to WASH and housing in urban/peri-urban slums in Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, and South Asia. Strictly quantitative studies and grey literature were excluded by design. Narrow Criterion 2 is rated borderline_narrow_c2 because legal/tenure/regulatory mechanisms (settlement legal status, land tenure security, landlord-tenant agreements, housing formalisation, eviction risk, and pay-per-use toilet pricing) are substantively synthesized in Sections 3.2, 3.3.3, and 3.3.4, but constitute one strand within a broader lived-experience scoping review where many included studies examine MHM stigma, gender roles, or physical latrine conditions rather than legal/institutional rules. 2. AMSTAR 2 Fit & Quality: AMSTAR 2 is a borderline fit for a JBI scoping review that neither aims to pool effect sizes nor conducts risk-of-bias appraisal. Under AMSTAR 2, confidence is Critically Low due to multiple critical flaws: unregistered protocol without RoB plan (Q2), no list of the 24 excluded full-text articles (Q7; note also Figure 1 PRISMA graphic renders blank on PDF p. 8), no RoB appraisal (Q9), and no consideration of RoB in synthesis (Q13), alongside single-reviewer full-text screening (Q5) and single-author data extraction (Q6). 3. Primary-Study Extraction & Bibliographic Audit: Appendices 1-4 (including the formal Appendix 4 data extraction table) are external online supplements not printed in the PDF, so included_studies_list_completeness is partial_inline_citations_only. However, auditing all empirical citations across Results Section 3 (excluding the external conceptual comparison Rigon, 2022 in 3.1 and the UN-Habitat grey-literature discussion paper Singh, S. D. et al., 2022 in 3.4.1) yields exactly 33 unique peer-reviewed journal articles (2000-2022), matching the reported N = 33 count 1-for-1. Note two reference-manager metadata corruptions in the published Reference list (PDF p. 20): both Kwiringira et al. (2014, BMC Public Health 14) and Munn et al. (2018, BMC Med Res Methodol 18) had their titles and DOIs overwritten with Article #1 of their respective BMC volumes.

review_design_self_description: systematic mapping (systematic map / evidence map with metadata coding and narrative synthesis)
methodological_notes: 1. Review Design & Criterion 3 Status: Although grounded in a published Campbell Systematic Reviews protocol (Macura et al., 2021), the authors deviated from a full systematic review to a CEE-style systematic map (evidence and gap map with metadata coding and descriptive frequency counts). They explicitly performed no critical appraisal and no outcome effect extraction ("This systematic map was also not set to evaluate the impacts of WASH interventions on GESI outcomes"). Consequently, AMSTAR 2 is only borderline-applicable ("borderline_scoping_realist_or_hybrid"), and overall confidence under AMSTAR 2 is "Critically Low" due to two critical omissions by design (Q9 and Q13: absence of risk-of-bias assessment and interpretation). 2. Narrow Criterion 2 Fit: Fails narrow Criterion 2 ("fails_narrow_c2_e03"). The map catalogues broad WASH interventions (behaviour change 50.5%, WASH infrastructure 40%, training/capacity building 24.8%) across 25 GESI outcome themes (equitable access, WASH knowledge, time use, participation, attitudes, MHM, empowerment). It does not examine legal, statutory, regulatory, tenure, property-right, or administrative rules governing the WASH "Legal Last Mile" (mentioning "affordability" [19.9%] and "financial support (such as the provision of tariffs, loans and subsidies) (13.5%)" of the 104 GESI-mainstreamed studies solely as high-level metadata frequency tags). 3. Minor Internal Reporting Discrepancy: The Abstract reports searching "16 bibliographic databases and 53 specialist websites", whereas Methods and Figure 1 report "15 bibliographic sources" and "57 organisations" (56 searched in English, 12 in Spanish). 4. Double-Counting Audit / Primary Studies: The map includes 463 studies across 499 publications, but ZERO included primary studies are named, tabulated, or cited anywhere in the main text, figures, or 59-item reference list; the entire dataset resides in online supplemental table S6 and an external EviAtlas webpage.

S372 (Nelson et al., 2021) is a theory-driven realist review following RAMESES publication standards rather than a conventional Cochrane/PRISMA effectiveness review. Searches were run across PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus in April 2019 and March 2021 (covering 2010-2020, English peer-reviewed primary studies in LMICs; grey literature excluded), with selection counts reported in the text and Figure 1 yielding 73 included studies across 29 countries. On narrow Criterion 2, the review is borderline: its primary exposure is community participation broadly (including behavioural CLTS shaming, peer diffusion, and hygiene education), but three of its five mechanisms (accountability, market, and ownership) and several of its 19 contextual factors examine local institutional governance rules, committee bylaws and management plans, fines/penalties for non-compliance or water-use limits, user fees/tariff enforcement, decision-making authority, and accountability to government water boards and guidelines. AMSTAR 2 is only borderline-fit for a realist synthesis and yields Critically Low confidence due to critical flaws in Q2 (no registered/a priori protocol), Q7 (no excluded full-text list), Q9 (explicit omission of formal risk-of-bias/quality appraisal in favour of RAMESES relevance/rigour screening), and Q13 (no incorporation of study RoB in interpretation). Although the formal summary table of study countries and intervention types was placed in an online supplemental appendix (hence partial_inline_citations_only), cross-checking all empirical LMIC citations in Table 2 and the Results synthesis (excluding theoretical/methodological citations) recovers all 73 unique included primary studies—including exact reconciliation of two duplicate bibliography entries (Kwangware et al. 2014 listed as both Ref 18 and Ref 93; Ganing et al. 2018 listed as both Ref 82 and Ref 128) and matching the reported regional breakdown (5 Latin American studies and 1 SIDS study).

review_design_self_description: narrative review with database search (Lancet Global Health Review)
methodological_notes: S418 (Brown et al., 2023) is a Lancet Global Health thematic/policy 'Review' equipped with a standard 4-sentence Lancet 'Search strategy and selection criteria' box (searching PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus with search terms in online appendix pp 1-3, no date/language restrictions, plus key reports, government documents, UN resolutions, and the authors' collective field experience). Substantively, it strongly satisfies narrow Criterion 2 (passes_narrow_c2): dedicated sections and panels examine racial municipal underbounding and annexation law (Panel 1), full-cost recovery tariff rules, involuntary water shutoffs/disconnections for unpaid bills, customer assistance programmes, and privatisation (pp. e608-e610), policies tying WASH provision to formal property ownership and housing tenure, eviction of informal Roma settlements lacking formal property rights (Panel 2), and ordinances criminalising septic non-compliance and public urination/defecation (pp. e608-e609). Methodologically, however, it is a narrative review rather than a systematic synthesis (amstar2_fit = inappropriate_not_systematic; AMSTAR 2 = Critically Low with critical flaws on Q2, Q7, Q9, and Q13): there is no protocol, no eligibility criteria, no screening process or PRISMA flow, no Results section, no study count, and no risk-of-bias appraisal. Because zero primary studies were formally selected into an included-studies sample (included_studies_count_reported = 0; none_printed), included_primary_studies is empty; the 91 narrative references mix UN documents, secondary reviews (e.g., Anthonj 2020, Guo 2019, Meehan 2020, Wutich 2022, Wolf 2018), commentaries, and illustrative empirical studies (e.g., Lockhart 2020 and Hunter 2021 in Panel 1; Rosa 2019 in Panel 2; Ares 2017 in Panel 3; Hall 2019 and Jackson 2019 in Panel 4; Hermans 2017 and Dhesi 2018 in Panel 5; and Filcak 2018, Mack 2017, Pierce 2020, Gibson 2020, and MacDonald Gibson 2022 in the text; Refs 71 and 74 also duplicate Murray et al. 2020).

1. Review design & AMSTAR 2 fit: Cooper et al. (2021) is a PRISMA/JBI-guided 'systematic scoping review' (companion to Behnke et al., 2020 on protracted displacement and Shackelford et al., 2020 on emergency displacement). It conducts broad multi-database and grey-literature searches and duplicate Covidence screening, with a PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1), but performs no risk-of-bias/quality appraisal of the 84 peer-reviewed studies (only AACODS credibility screening on 4 grey literature records) and synthesizes findings via unstratified study counts. Hence AMSTAR 2 fit is 'borderline_scoping_realist_or_hybrid' and overall AMSTAR 2 confidence is 'Critically Low' (critical flaws on Q2, Q7, Q9, Q13). 2. Narrow Criterion 2 audit: Fails narrow Criterion 2 (E03). The review broadly maps environmental health conditions, pathogen exposures (e.g., Vibrio cholerae, malaria, measles), and clinical outcomes in refugee/IDP camps 6 months to 2 years post-displacement. Although Table 12 includes a sub-bullet for 'Legal/policy environments' under institutional obstacles, the text cites only one healthcare-seeking survey regarding camp-confinement policies (Mohamed et al., 2014) alongside general NGO/municipal coordination and project-duration issues (UNICEF and Hydroconseil, 2017; Tota-Maharaj, 2016; Schuller and Levey, 2014), rather than empirically analyzing legal, regulatory, tenure, tariff, or ownership rules governing WASH access. 3. Primary-study list & double-counting alert: The review reports 88 included transitional-phase publications, whose full study-by-study extraction matrices reside in external online supplements S3 and S4 (not printed in the 39-page PDF). Forty-nine of the 88 included records (including all 4 grey literature items) are explicitly named inline across Section 3 Results and Tables 9-10 and are extracted here (excluding benchmark standards cited inside Table 9/10 right-hand columns and Discussion-only background citations such as Ziersch et al. 2017, Hashmi et al. 2019, and Abbas et al. 2018). Crucially, Table 5 reveals that 18 of the 88 'included studies' (20%) are themselves secondary literature/systematic reviews (e.g., Ramesh et al. 2015, De Buck et al. 2015, Kimbrough et al. 2012, Rebaudet et al. 2013, Cronin et al. 2008) and 2 are guidelines, creating substantial secondary-on-secondary overlap risk if treated as primary studies.

Self-described systematic review with PRISMA-style selection flow diagram (Figure 1), explicit Boolean search string across 7 bibliographic databases plus Google/Google Scholar and backward citation tracking, custom risk-of-bias scoring (Table 1), study characteristics table (Table 2), coping-strategy matrix (Table 3), and thematic narrative synthesis of 28 empirical cross-sectional/qualitative studies (30 publications, as Humplick et al. 1993 [16] + Madanat & Humplick 1993 [17] and Zérah 1998 [23] + Zérah 2000 [24] share datasets and were each counted as 1 study by the authors; all 30 publications are extracted in included_primary_studies to ensure complete overlap detection). Rated borderline_narrow_c2 because the review's primary inclusion criteria and synthesis target behavioural/economic household coping strategies and averting expenditures/willingness-to-pay for infrastructurally unreliable water supplies rather than legal or regulatory rules per se, although property ownership/land tenure (Abstract; Section 3.2), mandatory fixed utility bills/tariffs (Section 3.3), illegal pipe connections (Section 3.1.1), and regulatory oversight of pro-poor/informal water services (Gerlach & Franceys 2009 [39]; Discussion p. 16) appear as secondary sub-themes. Internal reporting discrepancies noted during audit: (1) text cross-references to Table 1 and Table 2 on pp. 4-5 are swapped; (2) text p. 5 reports 12 low, 13 moderate, and 3 high RoB studies, whereas Table 1 lists 11 low, 14 moderate, and 3 high RoB studies; and (3) Cook et al. (2016) [28] is included in Table 1, Table 3, and Results text (rural Kenya) but was inadvertently omitted from Table 2 (leaving 27 rows in Table 2). AMSTAR 2 overall confidence is Critically Low due to multiple critical flaws: no pre-registered protocol (Q2), no list of the 13 excluded full-text articles (Q7), an adapted reporting-heavy quality score that does not adequately assess observational confounding/selection/measurement bias (Q9), and lack of RoB-stratified interpretation despite heavy reliance on high-RoB studies in Results (Q13).

review_design_self_description: systematic review (PRISMA 2020-guided mixed scientific and government policy/regulatory synthesis using thematic, narrative, and descriptive analysis)
methodological_notes: 1. Scope & Criterion 2/3 fit: Self-described as a PRISMA 2020 'Systematic Review', this paper is functionally a hybrid city-level scoping/thematic and policy synthesis covering both scientific literature and Rwandan legal/regulatory documents on household fecal sludge management (FSM) in Kigali. It strongly satisfies narrow Criterion 2 by analyzing Rwanda's institutional mandates, 23 laws/policies/regulations/standards/guidelines (Section 3.4, Table 7), exhauster licensing and emptying service regulations, tariff/cross-subsidy rules, and landlord–tenant shared-latrine maintenance responsibilities. 2. Internal count discrepancy: Abstract, Section 2.1, and Section 2.3 report 73 included publications (40 scientific publications + 33 government publications), whereas Discussion (Section 4.1) and Conclusions (Section 5) inconsistently state 68 included publications (36 scientific + 32 government). 3. List completeness & primary-study overlap notes: All 40 included scientific publications are completely tabulated in Appendix A (Table A1) and Appendix B (Tables A2–A3) and extracted above (noting that 4 of the 40—[21], [44], [55], [67]—are themselves secondary reviews/syntheses). Of the 33 government publications, 23 regulatory/policy/standard documents are tabulated in Table 7 while the remaining 10 government statistical/sector/audit reports (e.g., NISR EICV4/EICV5/RPHC5/RDHS, MININFRA BLJSR, OAG 2016 audit, RBC 2024 report) are only cited inline; p. 3 states that all included publications are in Supplementary Materials, though p. 21 lists only Table S1 (PRISMA 2020 Checklist). DOIs are not printed in the reference list (only '[CrossRef]' hyperlinks). 4. Appraisal & reporting anomalies: Figure 1 (PRISMA 2020 flow diagram, p. 4) renders as blank boxes without text/counts in the published PDF, and Table A3 (p. 30) is titled 'JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for systematic reviews and research syntheses' but actually uses the 6-item JBI Checklist for Text and Opinion even when scoring included systematic/scoping reviews ([55], [67]).

Self-described realist review combining systematic database/grey-literature searching (8 databases + policy/government portals), explicit eligibility criteria, a PRISMA selection flow diagram (Figure 1, rendered as an image on p. 605), JBI + culturally adapted CREATE appraisal (Appendix A), and Indigenous collaborative 'yarning circles' with a Co-design Brains Trust. Two critical methodological caveats apply for Task I overlap and eligibility auditing: (1) Borderline Narrow Criterion 2 fit: Although the review defines policy as mandatory compliance with consequences, includes linkage to accountability mechanisms (e.g., regulation) as an inclusion criterion, and analyzes the non-enforceable legal status of the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines (ADWG) and lack of statutory human-right-to-water obligations across federal/state/local law, its primary research questions examine participatory co-design and integration of Indigenous knowledge in policy formulation rather than empirically testing legal, regulatory, tenure, or tariff rules governing last-mile WASH access. (2) Near-absence of primary empirical WASH studies among the 38 included sources: Table 1 lists 5 'peer-reviewed studies' and 33 grey literature files (24 government policy/strategy documents, 4 WSAA local case study vignettes, and 5 media releases/articles). Even within the 5 'peer-reviewed studies', only Wyrwoll et al. (2022) is an empirical water-quality/policy dataset analysis; Balasooriya et al. (2023) is itself a secondary literature review, Howey & Grealy (2021) is a legal/policy analysis appraised as expert opinion, Vanweydeveld & WSAA (2022) is an industry review report (not a peer-reviewed journal article, and also the apparent source of Case Study #1), and Moggridge & Thompson (2021) is an Indigenous perspective article (whose numbered superscript 42 in Table 1 was omitted from the alphabetical reference list). AMSTAR 2 is only borderline-fit for realist policy reviews and rates Critically Low due to lack of a registered protocol (Q2), no excluded-studies list (Q7), non-standard RoB assessment omitted entirely for 33/38 sources (Q9), and failure to incorporate appraisal flaws into result interpretation (Q13).

review_design_self_description: scoping review (following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, with adapted JBI critical appraisal)
methodological_notes: 1. Review design & AMSTAR 2 fit: Although framed and reported as a PRISMA-ScR scoping review, the review poses an intervention-effectiveness question ('effectiveness of behaviour change interventions in increasing the uptake of sewer connections'), executes dual screening with a PRISMA flow diagram, and conducts formal critical appraisal (adapted JBI Case Reports checklist), making it a scoping/effectiveness hybrid ('borderline_scoping_realist_or_hybrid'). Under AMSTAR 2 it rates 'Critically Low' due to lack of a pre-registered protocol (Q2), unjustified English-only restriction (Q4), absence of an inline individual excluded-studies list and conflicting table numbering for Supplementary Table 3 (Q7), use of a descriptive case-report checklist rather than a true NRSI risk-of-bias tool covering confounding/selection bias (Q9), and causal-style effectiveness conclusions drawn from uncontrolled project reports without weighting by RoB (Q13). 2. Narrow Criterion 2 fit ('borderline_narrow_c2'): The review explicitly targets 'last-mile' household sewer connectivity, operationalizing 'behaviour change interventions' broadly to include indirect subsidies/connection-fee waivers and Output-Based Aid, while Table 2 also documents statutory/regulatory connection mandates (e.g., Bahia Law 7307 of 1998, São Paulo 2002 connection mandate, Tamil Nadu 100-meter mandatory connection rule, contractor-resident agreements in Ecuador). However, legal/regulatory/tenure rules were not the primary eligibility criterion (the Abstract explicitly contrasts behaviour change against legal barriers), making narrow Criterion 2 borderline. 3. Primary-study double-counting & bibliographic audit: Although the review reports n = 11 included studies, these derive from only 7 unique source documents (only 1 peer-reviewed journal article, Sachet & Bilotta 2020 [30], and 6 institutional/World Bank reports). Five of the 11 included studies are country/city case studies extracted from a single World Bank secondary report (Kennedy-Walker et al., 2020 [9] — itself a flagship 'Connecting the Unconnected' synthesis likely in the Legal Last Mile corpus!). Additionally, the Pakistan Lodhran Pilot Project report is cited twice in the bibliography ([29] Robinson 2005 and [38] World Bank 2005) and mangled in Tables 1-2 as 'Rural, S.U., 2005. Sanitation in South Asia', Sachet (2020) is abbreviated 'MadC S' in Ref [30], and Figure 4 mislabels El Alto, Bolivia as 'Guayaquil, Bolivia'.

Self-described 'documentary and integrative review' of 94 documents (36 peer-reviewed scientific articles [38.3%], 30 institutional reports [31.9%], 20 governmental legal/regulatory decrees and plans [21.3%], and 9 technical reports/notes [9.6%]; note subcounts sum to 95 in the authors' text). Substantively, the review squarely satisfies narrow Criterion 2 by analyzing federal/state/municipal decrees (e.g., Brazil's Decree 7.053/2009 PNPSR, emergency municipal decrees), urban public-space criminalization/access rules, intergovernmental coordination, and Housing First/tenure integration governing WASH access for unhoused populations. Methodologically, however, it is a hybrid documentary-integrative policy review rather than a rigorous systematic review (Critically Low on AMSTAR 2): no protocol registration, no PRISMA diagram, no duplicate screening/extraction, no risk-of-bias assessment, and an implausible screening yield (95 records identified across Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and Google Scholar, with only 1 excluded to leave 94). Moreover, although eligibility criteria specified 2020-2024, pre-2020 sources (2009, 2010, 2016, 2017, 2019) are cited in the synthesis. The full inventory of 94 included documents resides in external Supplementary Material Table S1; only 35 distinct sources (16 peer-reviewed journal articles, 1 preprint, 1 book chapter, 1 IPEA survey note, and 16 governmental/institutional/media sources) are named in the text/tables and Reference list, all of which are extracted here for primary-study overlap auditing.
